lead: This unit explains how rigid bodies move and how forces change that motion. You will solve plane-motion problems by relative velocity and acceleration, by the instantaneous centre, and by force, energy and impulse methods. You will finish with the basic spring-mass vibration that follows from these laws.
about: The unit starts with the two simple rigid-body motions, translation and fixed-axis rotation (6.1). General plane motion is then built as translation plus rotation (6.2). Chapter 6.3 turns this into the relative velocity and relative acceleration equations; Chapter 6.4 gives the instantaneous-centre shortcut for velocities. The second half moves to kinetics: Chapter 6.5 applies Newton's second law and the moment equation to plane motion, Chapter 6.6 treats angular momentum and angular impulse, and Chapter 6.7 compares work-energy and momentum methods. Chapter 6.8 uses the same mass-spring ideas to describe free undamped vibration. The build is deliberate: geometry first, then forces, then the two work-energy and impulse shortcuts, then a short vibration application.

chapters.idea: A rigid body's motion can be separated into translation, where every point has the same velocity and acceleration, and fixed-axis rotation, where every point moves on a circle about the axis.
chapters.depth: Define rigid body, angular displacement θ (rad), angular velocity ω=dθ/dt (rad/s), angular acceleration α=dω/dt (rad/s²). Give the constant-α equations: ω=ω₀+αt, θ=ω₀t+½αt², ω²=ω₀²+2αθ. For a point at radius r from a fixed axis, v=ωr, tangential acceleration a_t=αr, normal acceleration a_n=ω²r. Use a sign convention for clockwise and anticlockwise. Some syllabi call fixed-axis rotation 'rotation about a fixed axis'.

figure.title: Rigid-body motion
figure.aria: A rigid body's motion splits into translation and fixed-axis rotation; rotation has tangential and normal acceleration at radius r.

chapters.example: A flywheel starts from rest with constant angular acceleration α=2.5 rad/s². Find its angular velocity and angular displacement after t=4.0 s. For a point 0.30 m from the axis at that instant, find the tangential and normal accelerations.
chapters.trap: Using v=ωr with ω in degrees per second, or reporting only a_t and forgetting a_n.
chapters.prereq: Unit 5 particle kinematics; angle and radian measure.
chapters.leave: General plane motion and force causes are in 6.2 and 6.5.

chapters.idea: General plane motion is translation of a chosen base point plus rotation of the body about that base.
chapters.depth: Define plane motion: every point stays in a plane parallel to a fixed plane. Write v_B=v_A+ω×r_{B/A}; in plane the relative velocity is ω r_{B/A}, perpendicular to AB. Write a_B=a_A+α×r_{B/A}−ω²r_{B/A}; the last term points from B to A. Treat rolling without slipping as v_G=ωR and a_G=αR, with contact point velocity zero. Some syllabi call this 'absolute and relative velocity'.

figure.title: General plane motion
figure.aria: Plane motion combines translation of a base point with rotation about that point to give the velocity and acceleration equations.

chapters.example: A wheel of radius 0.40 m rolls without slipping on a horizontal road. Its centre moves at 3.0 m/s. Find the angular velocity of the wheel and the speeds of the top point and the contact point.
chapters.trap: Adding ωR to every point in the same direction; for rolling without slip the contact point has zero velocity.
chapters.leave: Relative acceleration examples and instantaneous centre to 6.3 and 6.4.

chapters.idea: Two points on the same rigid body have velocities and accelerations linked by the body's rotation about one of them.
chapters.depth: Use v_B=v_A+ω×r_{B/A} and a_B=a_A+α×r_{B/A}−ω²r_{B/A}. Draw velocity and acceleration polygons. Solve by components along convenient axes. Cover slider-crank and four-bar velocity and acceleration at one position, using given lengths and angles. The normal term ω²r always points from B toward A; the tangential term αr is perpendicular to AB. Some syllabi list this as 'relative velocity method' and 'relative acceleration method'.

figure.title: Relative motion method
figure.aria: The relative-motion solution starts from a base point, writes the velocity equation, draws a polygon, solves components and then repeats for acceleration.

chapters.example: Bar AB is 1.2 m long and makes 30° with the horizontal. End A moves horizontally to the right at 2.0 m/s. End B is constrained to move vertically. Find the angular velocity of the bar and the velocity of B.
chapters.trap: Using the relative velocity magnitude as ωL when the velocity directions are not perpendicular to AB, or dropping the ω²r term in acceleration.
chapters.leave: Instantaneous centre as a velocity shortcut in 6.4; force calculations to 6.5.

chapters.idea: At any instant, plane motion can be treated as pure rotation about a point called the instantaneous centre, where the velocity is zero.
chapters.depth: Locate the instantaneous centre I by drawing perpendiculars to the velocity directions at two points; their intersection is I. For parallel velocities, I lies on the line joining the points in the ratio of speeds, or at infinity for pure translation. Then v=ωr about I, with r measured from I. Use it for velocity only; I has zero velocity but not zero acceleration, and it moves with time. Cover rolling wheel and a bar sliding on floor and wall. Some syllabi write 'instantaneous center of rotation' or 'ICR'.

figure.aria: A bar with end A moving right and end B moving down; perpendiculars meet at instantaneous centre I, with distances 1.2 m and 0.9 m.

chapters.example: At one instant, end A of a 1.5 m bar is at (0.9, 0) m and moves right at 2.0 m/s. End B is at (0, 1.2) m and moves down at 1.5 m/s. Locate the instantaneous centre and find the angular velocity of the bar.
chapters.trap: Using the instantaneous centre to find acceleration, or forgetting that the centre changes from one instant to the next.
chapters.leave: Acceleration analysis stays with 6.3; kinetic forces in 6.5.

chapters.idea: For plane motion, the resultant force gives the mass-centre acceleration and the resultant moment about the mass centre gives the angular acceleration.
chapters.depth: Use ΣF_x=m a_Gx, ΣF_y=m a_Gy, ΣM_G=I_G α. For fixed-axis rotation about O, ΣM_O=I_O α. Draw the free-body diagram and the kinetic diagram. Cover translation only (α=0), fixed-axis rotation, and rolling without slip. I_G is the mass moment of inertia about the centroidal axis; I_O=I_G+m d². D'Alembert's principle may be used by adding inertia force −m a_G and inertia couple −I_G α. Some syllabi call this 'kinetics of rigid bodies using Newton's second law'.

figure.title: Force and acceleration
figure.aria: The force solution goes from a free-body diagram to a kinetic diagram, then to the two Newton-Euler equations and a unit check.

chapters.example: A uniform cylinder of mass 10 kg and radius 0.20 m rolls without slipping on a horizontal plane. A horizontal force P=40 N pulls at the centre. Find the acceleration of the centre and the friction force.
chapters.trap: Forgetting the friction moment about G, or using I about the contact point when taking moments about G.
chapters.prereq: 6.1-6.2; Unit 4 mass moment of inertia; Unit 5 Newton's second law.
chapters.leave: Angular momentum and impulse in 6.6; energy in 6.7.

chapters.idea: The angular momentum of a rigid body in plane motion is I_G ω about its mass centre, and angular impulse changes it.
chapters.depth: Define angular momentum H_G=I_Gω and H_O=I_Oω for fixed-axis rotation. Angular impulse is ∫M dt; angular impulse-momentum is H₂−H₁=∫M dt. If the external moment about an axis is zero, H about that axis is conserved. Include simple eccentric impact only if time permits. Only a few universities teach the inertia tensor and Euler's equations; mention that general 3D rotation needs them, without derivation. Some syllabi call this 'moment-of-momentum' or 'angular impulse-momentum relations'.

figure.title: Angular impulse
figure.aria: A moment produces angular impulse, which changes angular momentum; if the moment is zero, angular momentum stays constant.

chapters.example: A flywheel has mass moment of inertia I=5.0 kg m² about its axis and spins at 20 rad/s. A brake applies a constant opposing moment of 10 N m. Find the time to stop and the angular impulse of the brake.
chapters.trap: Losing the sign of the impulse, or using I about a point that is not the rotation axis.

chapters.idea: Work done by forces and moments changes a rigid body's kinetic energy, while impulse changes its momentum; choose the method that avoids unknown internal forces or time.
chapters.depth: Use T=½m v_G²+½I_Gω². Work of a force is ∫F·dr; work of a couple is ∫M dθ. Include potential energy mgh and ½kx², conservation when only conservative forces do work. For rolling without slip, friction does no work. Impulse-momentum equations: m v_G1+Σ∫F dt=m v_G2; I_Gω₁+Σ∫M_G dt=I_Gω₂. Cover one impact or collision example if the syllabus includes impact of rigid bodies; only a few universities include rigid-body impact, so keep it short. Some syllabi call this 'work-energy principle' and 'impulse-momentum method'.

figure.title: Two shortcuts
figure.aria: A motion problem branches into the work-energy route for speed or distance and the momentum route for time or impulse.

chapters.example: A uniform disk of mass 8.0 kg and radius 0.25 m rolls without slipping down an incline from rest. The vertical drop is 1.2 m. Find the speed of its centre at the bottom. Take g=9.81 m/s².
chapters.trap: Leaving out ½I_Gω², or counting friction work when rolling without slip.
chapters.leave: Vibration energy in 6.8; 3D impact beyond scope.

chapters.idea: A mass pulled back by a spring or gravity oscillates with simple harmonic motion whose natural frequency is set by stiffness and mass.
chapters.depth: Define simple harmonic motion x=A sin(ω_n t+φ). For a mass m on a spring k, ω_n=√(k/m) rad/s; period T=2π/ω_n; frequency f=1/T. Use displacement, velocity v=Aω_n cos(...), acceleration a=−ω_n²x. Cover free undamped vibration only. Mention damping and resonance in one line if the syllabus asks. Some syllabi call this 'mechanical vibrations' or 'free vibration'.

figure.aria: A sinusoidal displacement-time graph for a 0.05 m amplitude and 20 rad/s angular frequency.

chapters.example: A 2.0 kg mass hangs on a spring of stiffness k=800 N/m. It is pulled down 0.05 m from equilibrium and released from rest. Find the angular frequency, period, frequency and maximum speed.
chapters.trap: Mixing ω in rad/s with f in Hz; using k in N/cm without converting to N/m.
chapters.leave: Damped and forced vibration beyond basics; energy method cross-check in 6.7.
